description: We are a Dhaka-based data and software team tackling the Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge. Combining Python, geospatial analytics, and interactive visualization, we aim to bridge resolution and sensor differences between NASA’s thermal anomaly datasets to build a unified, reliable wildfire and hotspot tracking tool. Looking for teammates skilled in GIS/remote sensing, ML, web development, or science storytelling to build a high-impact solution together!
summary: FireWatch is a web-based wildfire and burning activity analysis platform that harmonizes NASA's MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m) active fire hotspot records into a consistent spatial and temporal time series. Processing 22,070,048 active fire observations across 419 NASA FIRMS archives (2025–2026), FireWatch aggregates raw detections onto 6,123,259 standardized 0.1° × 0.1° spatial grid cells, calculates a calibrated Fire Radiative Power (FRP) intensity index, and flags statistical anomaly outbreaks. Through an interactive global wildfire map, a 365-day clickable burning activity calendar, sensor-comparison analytics, and one-click filtered CSV exports, FireWatch empowers researchers, land managers, and emergency responders to compare long-term burning patterns and detect unusual fire activity accurately.
details:
Source Code Repository: https://github.com/ahmedkhalid008/FireWatch-Harmonizing-Earth-s-Burning-History

Problem: NASA's MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m) satellite instruments provide extensive active fire hotspot records, but differences in spatial resolution, detection sensitivity, and observation characteristics create artificial jumps when comparing raw multi-year counts directly.

Our Solution: FireWatch is a multi-sensor wildfire analysis platform that reconciles MODIS and VIIRS active fire detections into a unified spatial and temporal framework, making long-term historical burning patterns comparable and actionable.

How It Works:

1. Data Ingestion: Automatically ingested and cleaned 419 NASA FIRMS CSV archives (202 MODIS + 217 VIIRS) covering 22,070,048 active fire detections from 2025–2026.

2. Spatial-Temporal Harmonization: Snapped raw coordinates onto 6,123,259 standardized 0.1° × 0.1° (~11 km) spatial grid cells and computed a normalized 0–100 Harmonized Intensity Index using log-scaled Fire Radiative Power (FRP) and sensor calibration weights.

3. Statistical Anomaly Detection: Evaluated a 365-day historical baseline (Mean: 622,638.0 | Std Dev: 174,420.8) and flagged 25 extreme burning outbreak days exceeding the μ + 1.5σ (884,269.2) threshold.

4. Interactive Visualization & Export: Built a responsive web dashboard featuring an interactive global hotspot map (top 3,500 high-intensity centroids), a 365-day clickable burning activity heatmap calendar, MODIS vs. VIIRS comparison charts, and one-click filtered CSV downloads.

Tools & Technologies Used:

- Data Engineering: Python, Pandas, NumPy

- Frontend & Visualization: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, React Leaflet, Recharts, Lucide React

- Basemap & Cloud Hosting: Esri World Dark Gray Canvas, Vercel

Creativity & Expected Impact: By combining sensor-aware grid harmonization with an intuitive GitHub-style 365-day burning calendar, FireWatch eliminates cross-sensor bias and helps climate researchers, land managers, and emergency responders distinguish normal seasonal burning from extreme anomalies.

AI Assistance Acknowledgment: Large Language Models (Google Gemini) and AI-assisted development tools (Google Antigravity) were utilized to assist with data pipeline scripting, UI scaffolding, and technical documentation. All NASA FIRMS satellite datasets, statistical computations, and final validations were executed and verified by the author.
